gaps: Length: the biography has about 9,990 words of prose by the lint count (block quotes and the sources list excluded), within the tier A range of 8,000–10,000.

Approved miracles: the miracles finally approved for the beatification (1614) and canonization (1622), and how many, were not found. The texts of Paul V’s brief of 24 April 1614 and of Gregory XV’s canonization bull were not read. The 18 Rótulo articles (1609–10) are listed as proposed only; the Rota decree of 2 Jan. 1614 does not list miracles. The dead-tree claim still rests on Lovat citing the bull.

Escorial: a letter to Doña Inés Nieto (‘after 17 Dec. 1577’, first published 1919) describes an audience with Philip II at the Escorial. Its authenticity could not be confirmed, so the meeting is not stated; it is mentioned once in the Note on the Sources.

Exhumation dates follow the Rótulo: 4 July 1583 (art. 97), November 1585 (art. 101), return 23 Aug. 1586 (art. 101), and March 1592 (Mariana de la Encarnación). Lovat’s 24 Nov. 1585 is no longer used; Ana de San Bartolomé’s ‘víspera y día de santa Catalina’ for the arrival in Ávila fits it but is not stated.

Calendar: the biography states only that the day after 4 Oct. 1582 was counted 15 Oct. (Inter gravissimas; Butler; CE) and that the feast is kept on 15 Oct., the day after her death in the new calendar. No further reason for the feast date was found.
Canonization year: 12 March 1622 (Silverio, Dicastery, CE). Butler’s 1621 is wrong and is not used.

Spanish accents: the Ribera quotations were checked against the Gili text of Ribera (archive.org) in the check pass. The text there reads ‘Válame Dios, qué cansada me siento; más ha de veinte años que nunca me acosté temprano, sino ahora’, ‘No tengas pena por mí, hija…’, and ‘¿Tengo yo de tener cosa propia? ¿aquí no me darán un poco de tierra?’. The Procesos give ‘¿Y aquí no me darán un poco de tierra?’ and ‘vámonos a Avila’ (no accent on Avila there). The Báñez words were checked against the Silverio text of Procesos I.

Deathbed: the exchange with Ana de San Bartolomé (‘Déjense de eso’) and Juana del Espíritu Santo is in one deposition only (Mariana de la Encarnación); the ‘little earth’ question is in three. Ribera’s ‘¿Tengo yo de tener cosa propia?’ is joined to it.

Identifications not made because the notes do not make them: Fray Antonio de Jesús at Medina in 1582 and Antonio de Heredia of Duruelo; Antonio Gaytán of the Seville journey and the father of Mariana de Jesús; the prioress María Bautista of Valladolid and the María Bautista who saw a rapture.

Traditions told with attribution: Juan de la Miseria’s portrait remark (Fuente via Zimmerman); the princess of Eboli at Pastrana and the archbishop of Seville kneeling (Reforma via Zimmerman); Gracián’s Madrid-or-Seville test (Yepes via Zimmerman); Pedro de Castro’s doubts (Stanbrook note); Clement VIII’s ‘This man is a Saint’ (Zimmerman note).

Lorenzo’s death: his daughter’s letters date it two days after the feast of St. John (June 1580); the Stanbrook note on Teresa’s vision of his soul gives a different timing. The vision is in the miracles list as tradition only.

Second-hand testimony: Ana de la Encarnación’s account of the paralysis opens ‘esto oyó decir esta testigo’ and is told as what she heard. The remark about God finishing in the young nuns in three months what he had not finished in her (Ana de la Trinidad, 1597, from a visitor) is hearsay and was cut from the story.

Not used: the 1581 Alcalá Constitutions (text not read); the Christmas Eve 1577 broken arm (Stanbrook note, unchecked); the shoe-throwing woman of Toledo and the ‘Bible’ remark (secondary footnotes); the letter of 11 Nov. 1576 is paraphrased only (Zimmerman’s translation).
Patronage of Spanish writers, headache sufferers and people ridiculed for their piety was not found and is omitted. The patron field uses santiebeati.it only.

The date of the conversion before the wounded Christ (often 1554) is not confirmed and is left out. Entry at the Incarnation (1535 against 1533/1534) and her age at her mother’s death are stated as conflicts in the Note on the Sources.
Yepes’s Life (1587) was not found; his words come only as quoted by Ribera’s editor and by Zimmerman.
Deathbed visions (dove, star, visitors in white, crystal globe, music, Ana’s vision of the Lord) are marked as legend or as one witness’s report.
Lovat (1912) has flagged errors (Clement VII; the doctorate). Lovat-only facts still used: the 1750 shrine, the heart and thorns, the apparitions, the dead tree, the kitchen rapture with fish.

Chapter locators checked against Lewis (1870) in the check pass: Life ch. 1 (martyrdom, mother), ch. 4 (leaving home), ch. 9 (wounded Christ, Augustine), ch. 11 (garden), ch. 20 (rapture), ch. 26 (‘veritable Book’, ‘covered with wounds’), ch. 29 (angel).
The 2024 tomb opening date (28 Aug.) and the claim that the study began in 2022 come from search snippets and are not used; the Aleteia article reports an interview with two radiographers.
No image has a verified rights page.

Length of her struggle with prayer: Teresa writes that she was ‘a year and more without praying’ (Life 7:17), and that she spent nearly twenty years falling and rising on ‘this stormy sea’. The first draft said she gave up prayer ‘for years’; the check pass corrected this throughout. Báñez, who knew her later, said she had no faults beyond those of other good nuns and more prayer than most.

Corrections made in the check pass: ‘dos piedras vivas’ is Ribera’s phrase, not hers; the Medina del Campo scene now follows Foundations ch. 3 (the nuns watched Mass through the chinks of a door; the tapestries were the owner’s); ‘Ana de Jesús’, not Ana de la Encarnación, said ‘personas encapotadas y oraciones estrujadas’; Mary of the Nativity, not Mariana of the Angels, described Teresa writing with a resplendent face; Quiroga spoke to Teresa in Gracián’s hearing, not to Gracián alone; the Princess of Eboli’s part in the Inquisition’s demand rests on the chronicle quoted by Zimmerman, not on Ana de Jesús.
